title: Throat pairs: ح/ه · ع/ء · ح/خ

bigIdea.text: Six letters live in the throat, two at each level. To new ears ح/ه, ع/ء and ح/خ can sound alike, but each is a different letter: swap them and you change the word.

proper.text: Three levels, two letters each: the deepest part of the throat (nearest the chest) gives ء and ه; the middle gives ع and ح; the part nearest the mouth gives غ and خ.

ح vs ه: ه is an open, relaxed breath from the deepest part of the throat. ح comes from the middle of the throat: squeezed, stronger and sharper, but with no scrape. If you hear no difference, your ح is too relaxed.
ع vs ء: ء is 'strong' (shiddah): its sound stops completely, one clean catch. ع is 'in between' (tawassut): its sound neither stops fully nor flows fully.

provenance.title: صفة حرف (العربية) (Sifat of Arabic letters) — Arabic Wikipedia

proper.text: ح vs خ: both are whispered, but خ comes from higher up, near the mouth, is heavy, and has a light scrape. ح is light and smooth.

Common mistakes. Persian/Urdu readers merge ح into ه, and ع into ء or a plain vowel. English speakers often drop ع and ء, and say ح as a plain 'h'. Train the ear first: listen to each pair until you always hear the difference, then say it.

extras.text: A hand check: rest your fingers lightly on your throat. ع should buzz (voice) and ح should not, although both come from the middle of the throat.

tip.text: ه: relax the throat and breathe out, as in a sigh. ح: squeeze the middle of the throat and push the breath through: stronger and sharper, never scraping.
ء: close the throat and release it in one clean catch. ع: squeeze the middle of the throat and let a voiced sound continue for a moment.
Start with a smooth ح in the middle of the throat, then move up toward the mouth and add a light scrape: that is خ, and it is heavy.

drills.prompt: Alternate the pairs: هَ حَ — ءَ عَ — حَ خَ

questions.q: Which pair comes from the SAME level of the throat?
explain: Right: both come from the middle of the throat.
ḥa is the middle of the throat; ha is the deepest part.
ʿayn is the middle; hamza is the deepest part.
ḥa is the middle; kha is the part nearest the mouth.

questions.q: You can't hear a difference between your ح and your ه. What is usually wrong?
options: The ح is too relaxed: squeeze the middle of the throat
explain: Right: ḥa needs the squeeze.
ha is meant to be soft; the fix is in ḥa.
Neither letter whistles.
The lips are not involved.

questions.q: What separates ء from ع in their sifat?
options: ء stops fully (strong); ع is in between
ء is whispered; ع is not
explain: Right: hamza is shiddah, ʿayn is tawassut.
Neither is whispered: both hold the breath back (jahr).
Neither whistles; the whistling letters are ص ز س.
Their sifat differ.

questions.q: Persian/Urdu readers often merge ع into…
explain: Right: the squeeze of ʿayn gets lost.
ghayn is a gargle; that is not the usual merge.
ḥa shares ʿayn's place, but the usual merge is with hamza.
ha is the usual merge for ḥa, not for ʿayn.

questions.q: Which of these throat letters is heavy?
explain: Right: kha is one of the seven heavy letters.
ḥa is light.
ha is light.
ʿayn is light.

questions.q: Which English expression has a sound like ء in the middle?
explain: Right: the catch between 'uh' and 'oh' is a hamza-like stop.
'ahead' has an 'h' (like ه) in the middle.
'hello' starts with an 'h'.
'loch' has a scrape like خ.

options: The deepest part of the throat, nearest the chest
The part of the throat nearest the mouth
explain: Right: ha shares this place with ء.
That is the place of ع and ح.
That is the place of غ and خ.
The back of the tongue makes ق and ك.

questions.q: Which two letters come from the part of the throat nearest the mouth?
explain: Right.
They come from the middle of the throat.
They come from the deepest part of the throat.
They come from the back of the tongue, not the throat.

questions.q: Your ح sounds like خ. What fixes it?
options: Bring it down to the middle of the throat and remove the scrape
Raise the back of the tongue
explain: Right: ḥa is smooth.
That makes it heavier, more like kha.
Voice turns it toward ʿayn or ghayn.
The lips are not used.

questions.q: Your ع sounds like ء. What fixes it?
options: Keep a squeezed, voiced sound going from the middle of the throat
explain: Right: ʿayn continues a little; hamza stops dead.
A sharper catch makes it even more like hamza.
Whispering turns it into ḥa.
The lips are not used.

questions.q: What do ح and ه have in common?
options: Both are whispered: the breath flows
Both are strong: the sound stops
explain: Right: both are in the whispered (hams) group.
Neither stops; both are soft (rakhawa).
Neither is a qalqalah letter.
Neither whistles.

questions.q: With your fingers resting on your throat, which letter of the pair ع/ح should buzz?
explain: Right: ʿayn is voiced.
ḥa is only breath.
Only ʿayn buzzes.
ʿayn does buzz.

questions.q: Which pair do Persian/Urdu readers most often merge into a plain 'h'?
explain: Right: both become 'h'.
ʿayn and hamza merge as a catch or a vowel, not 'h'.
ghayn and kha are not merged into 'h'.
kha and kaf are not merged into 'h'.

remnote: ح vs ه == ح: squeezed breath from the middle of the throat; ه: relaxed breath from the deepest part
ع vs ء == ع: squeezed voiced sound, middle of the throat, in between; ء: one clean catch that stops, deepest part
ح vs خ == ح: smooth and light, middle of the throat; خ: light scrape, heavy, nearest the mouth
Throat levels == Deepest: ء ه; middle: ع ح; nearest the mouth: غ خ
